newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia, U.S. agency settle power dispute.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia, U.S. agency settle power dispute.

text.p: British Columbia said on Wednesday it settled a dispute with the U.S. Bonneville Power Administration with a deal under which the Canadian province will receive 1,400 megawatts of power.

British Columbia said it expects to sell the power for up to C$5 billion over the 27-year year life of the accord. The deal also gives the province's hydroelectric authority equal access to the U.S. market, eliminates special transmission rates for power crossing the B.C.-U.S. border and eliminates the need for a new transmission line in British Columbia.

The dispute arose last year when the BPA walked away from a 1994 agreement in principle which would have required it to pay British Columbia C$250 million and 950 megawatts of power. It said falling electricity prices made the deal uneconomic.
British Columbia built three dams on the Columbia River in the 1960s that were paid for by the United States but managed by the B.C. hydroelectric authority.

Under the Columbia River Treaty, those dams provided water for power generation in the United States. Half the power belonged in principle to British Columbia but the province sold its rights to the power to Bonneville in a deal that expires in 1998.
The current dispute centers on what will happen after 1998 when British Columbia is to get its share of the power back.
Under the new deal, British Columbia will get no cash upfront and will have to sell the 1,400 megawatts -- enough for 500,000 homes -- in the United States or use it domestically.

Opposition British Columbia politicians said the government was overestimating the potential revenues the power might generate. Premier Glen Clark said the current deal provides benefits equal to or greater than the 1994 agreement.
